case_name: Government of Andhra Pradesh and others v Ch. Gandhi
petitioner: Government of Andhra Pradesh and others
respondent:
Ch. Gandhi
Supreme Court of India

19 February 2013
C.A. No. 1427-1428 of 2013 .
The Judgment was delivered by : Dipak Misra, J.
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeals by special leave are directed against the judgment and order dated 14.6.2007 passed by the High Court of Judicature, Andhra Pradesh at Hyderabad in Writ Petition No. 12177 of 2007 and the order dated 8.2.2008 passed in Review WPMP (SR) No. 126152 of 2007 arising from the said writ petition whereby the Division Bench overturned the order dated 16.5.2007 passed by the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad (for short "the Tribunal") in O.A. No. 923 of 2006 on the ground that the disciplinary authority had imposed two major penalties. Be it noted, the High Court granted liberty to the department to pass appropriate orders keeping in view the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1991 (for short "the Rules").
3. The facts which are imp
facts: The disciplinary proceeding under Rule 5 of the Rules was initiated against the respondent, a Senior Accountant in the Office of the Sub Treasury, Nakrekal.
A disciplinary proceeding was conducted and the respondent was found guilty of misconduct.
The penalty imposed by the disciplinary authority was reversion to the post of Junior Accountant for two years with the stipulation that there would be postponement of future increments.

The respondent approached the Tribunal in O.A. No. 923 of 2006 and raised various points assailing the validity of the initiation of the proceeding, the manner in which the enquiry was conducted and lastly, that the punishment imposed was disproportionate to the misconduct.
The High Court granted liberty to the department to pass appropriate orders keeping in view the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1991.
issues: Were the charges framed against the respondent proved?
Was the punishment imposed by the disciplinary authority disproportionate to the misconduct?
Did the High Court err in holding that two major penalties were imposed in violation of the Rules?
petitioner_arguments: The punishment was in consonance with the Rules and further such imposition of punishment not being unknown to service jurisprudence, did not warrant interference by the High Court.
The amended Rules permit imposition of such punishment but the same has not been taken note of by the High Court which makes the order absolutely vulnerable.
respondent_arguments: The interpretation placed by the High Court on the Rules cannot be found fault with inasmuch as the language employed in the Rules is absolutely plain, clear and unambiguous.
Under the Rules, imposition of two major penalties is not permissible.

When the language employed in the Rules has been differently couched and both the employer and employee are bound by the Rules, what could be jurisprudentially permissible need not be adverted to in this case.
court_reasoning: After a detailed examination of the inquiry report and the explanation of the charged officer, the disciplinary authority finds that the charges framed against Sri Ch. Gandhi the then Senior Accountant and incharge Sub Treasury Officer, Sub Treasury (non-banking) Nakrekal have been proved.
The relevant part of Rule 9 which provides for major penalties is as follows: ...
Sub-rule (27) of Rule 11 which has been relied on by the High Court reads as follows: ...
It is necessary to scrutinize the Rule position after the amendment on 6.12.2003.
holding: The punishment could be imposed in accord with the amended Rules or under the unamended Rules.
The respondent would be governed under the new Rules as cl. (vii) of Rule 9 has been substituted and the term 'substituted' conveys that the Rule has retrospective effect.
Even if the Rules are not treated as retrospective, the appellant had no vested right to be imposed a particular punishment under the unamended Rules.
